title: Require a technically-enforced acceptable-use policy before permitting employee use of third-party generative AI tools
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the Samsung ChatGPT data leak. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

decision_statement: Before employees are permitted to use third-party generative AI tools on company devices or with company data, the organisation must publish a specific acceptable-use policy defining what data categories may never be entered, and back it with a technical control (e.g. data-loss-prevention tooling or an approved enterprise-tier tool with contractual no-retention terms) rather than relying on policy text alone.
decision_context: Motivated by Samsung employees pasting confidential source code and internal meeting notes into a consumer-tier ChatGPT account within weeks of an internal ban being lifted, with no technical control preventing it.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Enterprise AI Use Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Publish a policy document without any technical enforcement.
Ban all third-party generative AI tools outright rather than defining an acceptable-use boundary.

citations.title: Samsung Bans ChatGPT, Google Bard, Other Generative AI Use by Staff After Leak

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this leak.
The decision is put into practice via this design pattern.
A published, technically-enforced policy is a concrete accountability structure for managing this class of AI risk.
Compliance must be demonstrated by attestation and technical-control records.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether the policy is technically enforced, not just written.
